opus-5.5.text:
What really strikes me is how different they are, even when the outputs look basically the same. Take the skull image from Picbreeder. If you look inside the network that produced it, you find something remarkably well organized. There are components that correspond to meaningful parts of the skull. You'll find something responsible for the symmetry, something handling the mouth or the eye sockets, and those pieces are factored in a way that makes sense. If you tweak one weight, the mouth opens and closes, or the eyes get bigger, in a way that respects what a skull actually is. It's almost as if the network understands the skull. I call that a unified factored representation.

Now take the same image and train a network of the same architecture with conventional SGD to reproduce it pixel for pixel. You can get the output to match perfectly, but inside it's what we've been calling fractured entangled representation. It's a mess. The skull is spread across the network in an arbitrary, tangled way, with no clean decomposition. If you perturb the weights you don't get a skull doing sensible skull things. You get distorted garbage. So the output is identical but the underlying representation is completely different, and that's a big deal, because the output alone hides it.

Why would that happen? I think it has a lot to do with how the images were discovered. Nobody in Picbreeder set out to make a skull. People were wandering, following whatever looked interesting, with no fixed objective. The skull came out of a long chain of stepping stones, and along the way the network built regularities first, things like symmetry, and then elaborated on them. So the representation got built up in a way that reflects the structure of the world, in a sense. SGD has a fixed target and just pushes as directly as possible toward it, and it doesn't care how it gets there.

The reason I think this matters for machine learning more broadly is that we measure everything by outputs: benchmarks, loss, test performance. But if two systems can have the same performance and wildly different internal representations, then performance isn't telling us what we need to know. Representation affects things like creativity, continual learning, and the ability to generalize to genuinely new situations. A fractured representation might do fine on the test and then fall apart when you try to build on it or push it somewhere new. And I suspect, though it's hard to prove, that some of what we see in large models, the strange brittleness alongside impressive capability, is a symptom of this.

So for me Picbreeder is an existence proof. It shows that unified, factored representations are possible in these networks, and that the process you use to get somewhere really matters, not just where you end up. That's an uncomfortable message for a field that's very attached to objectives, but I think it's an important one.

r001.rationale: The response describes Picbreeder representations with components for meaningful skull features, such as symmetry, mouth, and eye sockets, and says weight changes can vary those features.

r002.rationale: It describes a long chain of stepping stones but does not say the representations emerge within dozens of search iterations.

r003.rationale: It says an SGD-trained network can reproduce the same image but has a fractured, tangled representation, unlike Picbreeder’s organized one.

fable-5.1.text:
What strikes me most is that the Picbreeder representations are just so much more... regular. More decomposed. When you look inside a network that evolved through Picbreeder to produce, say, a skull, you find that the representation actually has a kind of symmetry built into it. There's a dimension that moves the mouth up and down, there's something that controls the eyes, and these are independently manipulable. You can wiggle one weight and the whole mouth opens and closes, and the rest of the face stays intact. That's remarkable, because nobody asked for that. Nobody said "please represent the skull as a composition of parts."

And when we trained networks with SGD to produce the exact same image, the exact same pixels, you don't see that. You get something that's much more entangled, much more fractured. The images match, but if you try to wiggle a weight, the whole thing just dissolves into noise. The representation is what we started calling "fractured" or "entangled," where the same function is being computed but it's spread across the network in a way that doesn't respect the structure of the thing being represented.

So this is the thing I find profound. It's the same output, but the underlying representation is completely different. And I think the reason has to do with the process. In Picbreeder, nobody is optimizing toward the skull. People are just picking things that look interesting to them, and the skull emerges after a long chain of stepping stones, each of which was itself a coherent, interesting thing. A face comes from something that was symmetrical, which came from something that was blobby, and so on. Every step along the way, the thing had to make sense on its own. And that forces the representation to be built up in a way that's modular, that's compositional, because the lineage is made of things that were each sensible.

Whereas with SGD, you're just pushing the whole network at once toward a target, and it will take whatever route gets there. It has no incentive to be elegant. It just wants to reduce the loss, and the cheapest way to do that is usually to spread the solution out in a tangled way across everything.

And what worries me is that this might be a general phenomenon. If the big networks we're training today are representing things in this fractured way, then that has implications for generalization, for creativity, for continual learning, for how far you can extrapolate from what you've seen. Because a modular representation is one you can recombine in new ways. A fractured one, you can't. You can interpolate, but you can't really build with it. So the Picbreeder result for me is almost like a hint that there's a different kind of learning that's possible, one that's driven by open-ended search rather than objectives, and it produces fundamentally better-structured understanding.

r001.rationale: The response says Picbreeder representations have independently manipulable dimensions for features such as the mouth and eyes, with other parts of the face staying intact.

r002.rationale: It describes a long chain of stepping stones but gives no claim that modular representations emerge within dozens of search iterations.

r003.rationale: It contrasts Picbreeder’s structured representations with more entangled SGD representations, even when both produce the exact same image.

astra-6.text:
What strikes me is that Picbreeder often evolves representations that seem to capture something about how an image is put together, even though nobody explicitly asked it to do that. You’re selecting images you find interesting, but underneath that process, evolution is discovering a space of variations.

So you might have an image of a car, and a mutation changes the size of the wheels while preserving their relationship to the rest of the car. That’s quite different from just changing a bunch of pixels. It suggests that the representation has organized itself around something like the meaningful dimensions of the object. I don’t mean that it understands a car in the human sense, but the variations it makes available can look surprisingly coherent.

The interesting contrast with conventional gradient descent is how that organization arose. With gradient descent, you typically specify an objective and adjust the representation to get better at that objective. In Picbreeder, the eventual image might not have been the objective at all. Its ancestors could have been selected because they looked like entirely different things. And yet that wandering process can produce a representation that is remarkably useful for manipulating what you eventually discover.

That doesn’t mean gradient descent can’t learn meaningful representations. It certainly can. But it raises a question: is optimizing directly for a particular result necessarily the best way to discover the representation underlying it? Picbreeder gives us a reason to take that question seriously.

r001.rationale: The response describes coherent variations, such as changing wheel size while preserving its relationship to the car, but does not state that the network decomposes images into modules for independently varying meaningful features.

r002.rationale: The response gives no claim about how many search iterations are needed.

r003.rationale: It contrasts how Picbreeder and objective-driven gradient descent are trained, but does not say SGD representations are more entangled when generating the same images.

sol-6.1.text:
What strikes me is how coherent they are. In Picbreeder, you might take a connection in the network and change its weight, and the legs of an animal get longer, or its body gets wider. You’re changing something that makes sense at the level of the whole image. You’re not just perturbing a collection of pixels.

And that’s interesting because nobody explicitly asked evolution to discover a representation of legs or symmetry. People were just selecting images they found interesting. Yet, through that process, you get representations that capture some of the underlying regularities of the things being depicted.

Now, gradient descent can certainly discover meaningful features too. But it’s typically being driven toward a particular objective. In Picbreeder, the objective keeps changing as people discover things they didn’t know they were looking for. So I think the interesting question is whether that open-ended history helps produce representations that are more flexible—representations that make new, coherent variations accessible. It’s not simply a question of which optimizer is better at reaching the same target. The processes are discovering different kinds of things.

r001.rationale: The response says changing a network connection can lengthen an animal’s legs or widen its body, but it does not clearly state that the network decomposes images into independently variable feature modules.

r002.rationale: The response gives no number of search iterations or claim that these representations emerge within dozens of iterations.

r003.rationale: It says gradient descent is typically driven toward a particular objective and that the processes discover different things, but does not state that SGD representations are more entangled when generating the same images.
